The Coefficients of a Fitted Model

Source: R/report.R
coef.StatmodFit.Rd

Returns one named vector per distribution parameter: the quantities in which the model is written, or the coordinates on which it was estimated.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'StatmodFit'
coef(object, readable = TRUE, ...)

Arguments

object

A StatmodFit().

readable

TRUE, the default, reports the quantities in which the model is written. FALSE reports the coordinates on which it was estimated.

...

Unused.

Value

A named list with one entry per distribution parameter, in the family's order, each a named numeric vector. The names are the coefficient labels, composed from each term's own label, so two terms of one kind in one formula stay apart.

What readable moves, and what it does not

Most coefficients are the same under either reading: the coefficient of a linear predictor is reported as it is estimated. Three kinds of term report quantities that differ from the coordinates on which they are carried, and those are the parameters that this argument moves.

A break-point term is fitted through a working block, and its quantities are read from that block. A continuous term holds each quantity as a coefficient, and the two readings coincide. A discontinuous term carries \(g\) and \(\delta\); where its position is not held, it reports \(\psi = -g/\delta\), so that at readable = FALSE the vector holds \(g\), which is no quantity of the model. Where the term holds its position, as a sharp jump() or jseg() does after the fit has settled it, the reported position is the held one.

A score-driven term carries its level and its loadings \(\kappa_j\) through their own links, the log for a loading, and its persistence on partial autocorrelations, because the stationary region is not a box. Each partial autocorrelation is carried on the unconstrained scale of its link, the inverse hyperbolic tangent by default. The quantity \(\xi_j\) of the literature is the autoregressive coefficient that the whole chart produces. With one persistence, \(\xi_1\) is the partial autocorrelation. With two, \(\xi_1 = \mathrm{pacf}_1 (1 - \mathrm{pacf}_2)\) and \(\xi_2 = \mathrm{pacf}_2\).

A regime term is estimated on the additive log-ratios of each row of its transition matrix, and it reports the transition probabilities \(p_{ij}\) in their place. Its levels and gaps are reported through their own links.

Where a term declares no quantities of its own, the coordinates stand. So do the coefficients of a parameter developed over covariates: a development is a vector with no single value to report, so the term declares nothing for it.

A structural term is present under both readings

A structural term contributes no design columns, so its parameters are in no block of the design. Both readings append them to the vector of the equation, so that a model whose whole predictor is a score-driven filter returns its filter parameters.

The coordinates of the fit

readable = FALSE gives the coordinates on which the fit was estimated, with a structural term's part on the unconstrained scale that its charts define. For a model without a structural term, this vector has the order of the rows of vcov(object, readable = FALSE), and it can be passed as the par argument of loglik() or to an optimizer. A structural level that is held appears in the vector at its held value and has no row in that matrix.

Hyperparameters are not coefficients and are not here. hyper() reports them.

See also

hyper() for the hyperparameters, vcov.StatmodFit() for the variance matrix, whose rows with readable = FALSE are the coordinates of coef(object, readable = FALSE) that are not held, summary.StatmodFit() for the two together, modelterms7::term_readable() for what a term declares.

Examples

set.seed(1)
d <- data.frame(x = sort(runif(200, 0, 10)))
d$y <- 0.3 * d$x + 1.5 * pmax(d$x - 6, 0) + rnorm(200, 0, 0.4)
fit <- statmod(y ~ modelterms7::seg(x, psi = 4),
               distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), d)

# The break-point is a quantity of the model, near the true 6.
coef(fit)$mu
#> (Intercept)    seg.beta  seg.gamma1    seg.psi1 
#> -0.05693875  0.31903803  1.54956901  6.13040161 

# The coordinates on which the fit ran are the same numbers here, because
# seg() is continuous, and vcov() has one row for each of them.
coef(fit, readable = FALSE)$mu
#> (Intercept)    seg.beta  seg.gamma1    seg.psi1 
#> -0.05693875  0.31903803  1.54956901  6.13040161 
rownames(vcov(fit, readable = FALSE))
#> [1] "mu:(Intercept)"    "mu:seg.beta"       "mu:seg.gamma1"    
#> [4] "mu:seg.psi1"       "sigma:(Intercept)"
